MODAL_CAN.text: The library committee wanted to make quiet study easier. For one week, Mei and Koki counted how many seats were used before school and after school. In the morning, most students sat near the windows because the light was good. After school, those seats were often noisy because club members met near the entrance. The committee had planned to put all the ‘Quiet Study' signs by the windows. However, the survey showed a different need. They moved two signs to the back tables for after-school users and left one sign near the windows for the morning. A second count three days later showed that more students chose the quiet area. The committee learned that the best place for a sign can change with time.

MODAL_COULD.text: On Monday, the class received the same festival message twice. One copy came from the student council list, and another came from the class event list. Some students thought the second message included new information, so they read both carefully. Aya compared the two messages and found that every detail was the same. She asked the teachers who managed the lists. They learned that both lists included all second-year students. Before the next event, the class chose one list for general notices and kept the other only for messages about class jobs. They also added a short line saying where each message came from. The next notice arrived only once, and students could understand its purpose immediately. A small change made communication clearer.

MODAL_COULD.text: A new water station was placed outside the gym. During the first week, students often formed a long line after practice. Some people said the machine was too slow and should be replaced. The health committee decided to check before making that request. They measured how long it took to fill ten bottles. The machine itself worked at almost the same speed each time. Then they watched the line. A small table for bags stood directly beside the station, so students had to turn and wait for one another before they could leave. The committee moved the table two meters away and marked a separate place for waiting. The next afternoon, the same number of students used the station, but the line moved much faster. The school did not need a new machine. Careful observation showed that the space around it, not the machine, caused most of the delay. Before moving anything, they also asked two students to describe where the line felt slow. Both pointed to the narrow space beside the table, not to the water flow. This matched the timing results and gave the committee another reason to test the layout first.

MODAL_COULD.text: The art club made a poster for its open room. They placed it low on a wall near the stairs because the colors looked bright there. During lunch, however, few students entered. Yuto stood in the crowded hallway to see why. Bags and students blocked the lower wall, and he could not read the club name from several meters away. The members tested the same poster in two higher places. They asked ten students to walk from the stairs and say when they noticed it. More students saw it early when it was at eye level near the corner. The club moved the poster there instead of printing a larger one. The next day, more visitors found the room.

PARTICIPLE_POSTMODIFIER.text: The school library offered two ways to borrow a tablet. One card showed four written steps. Another had a QR code that opened a guide. Older students used either method easily, but many first-time users asked the same questions. Nana watched them and noticed a problem. The written card used ‘device number' before showing where that number was. The online guide showed the number first but hid the return rule on its last page. The committee combined the useful parts. A new card used one photo, three short steps, and one clear return rule. A QR code remained for students who wanted more detail. After the change, fewer users needed help, while both borrowing methods stayed available.

MODAL_COULD.text: The student council was preparing a guide for visitors who used wheelchairs. Two routes led from the school gate to the hall. Route A was thirty meters shorter, so the first draft called it the better route. Before printing the guide, Miki suggested walking both routes after rain. The next wet morning, the team checked them with a teacher. Route A crossed a smooth stone area near the garden. Water stayed there, and one part was slippery. Route B was longer, but it had a covered path and a gentle ramp with a rough surface. The team also timed both routes. Route B took only two minutes longer. They changed the guide to recommend Route B on rainy days and added a note about Route A for dry weather. The shortest route was not always the safest or most useful one. The team wrote both results in the guide instead of calling one route good and the other bad. That way, visitors could understand why the rainy-day recommendation was different and could choose with the weather in mind.

ADJECTIVE_TO_INFINITIVE.text: The lost-and-found box near the office stayed full for weeks. Every Friday, the student council posted a list, but few owners came. Ryo interviewed six students who had lost items. They said the list was hard to use. It included words such as ‘small bag' or ‘blue object,' but several things matched them. The council changed the recording card. Staff now wrote where an item was found, one special feature, and the date. For example, ‘blue pencil case with a white star, found by the gym on May 12' was clear. The next two lists used the new details. More items were returned, and the box finally had space. Better information worked better than reminders alone.

MODAL_COULD.text: At the school festival, two food stands sold different snacks. Visitors kept choosing Stand B because its line looked shorter. However, some of them later said they had waited longer there. The festival team wanted to know why. They counted people in each line every five minutes and also measured the time from ordering to receiving food. Stand A usually had twelve people waiting, but each order took about forty seconds. Stand B often had only seven people, yet each order took nearly ninety seconds because one snack had to be heated after the order. The team put a small sign at both stands showing the usual preparation time. They also prepared part of Stand B's snack before the busiest period. Visitors could then choose with better information, and the longest waits became shorter. Line length alone had hidden the real cause. The team checked again during the final hour to see whether the change only worked once. Stand B still had fewer people in line than Stand A, but its waiting time was now close to the time shown on the sign. The second check supported their explanation.

PAST_PROGRESSIVE.text: Visitors often stopped at the campus map near the front gate and then walked in the wrong direction. The map was correct, so volunteers first planned to add arrows. Sora watched five visitors use it. The top of the map showed north, but people at the gate were facing south. Some turned left on the paper and then turned left with their bodies, although those directions were different. The team printed a test copy rotated to match the view from the gate. They asked five more visitors to find the science room. Four chose the correct path without help. The team kept a small north mark but used the visitor's view as the main direction. Rotating the map worked better than adding many arrows.

WH_TO_INFINITIVE.text: Group work in Class 2-1 often began slowly. Students spent several minutes moving chairs, finding papers, and asking what to do. The teacher suggested a three-minute quiet setup before discussion. Some students thought silence would waste time, so the class tested it for four lessons. During those three minutes, everyone read the task, prepared materials, and wrote one idea alone. The class recorded when each group began real discussion. Before the test, most groups needed about six minutes to start. With the quiet setup, they usually started in four minutes, including the silent time. Students also entered the discussion with an idea ready. The class kept the setup because it gave everyone a clear first step.

MODAL_COULD.text: A school charity group placed a donation box near the entrance with a sign that said, ‘School supplies welcome.' After a week, the box contained many things the group could not use, including broken pens, opened paint, and very large notebooks. The students did not want to blame the donors. They checked the rejected items and asked three families what they thought ‘school supplies' meant. The answers were different. The group replaced the broad phrase with four clear examples: unopened pencils, clean erasers, A4 notebooks, and rulers under thirty centimeters. It also added two small pictures showing items that could not be accepted. During the next collection week, the total number of donations was a little lower, but almost every item could be used. Clear examples made the rule easier to understand and reduced waste for the volunteers who sorted the box. The group kept the old sign in its meeting notes so members could compare the two versions later. They also decided to review the accepted-item examples before the next season, because the needs of the receiving group might change.

WANT_TO.text: The basketball team planned a ninety-minute practice before an important game. The schedule had three drills with no break because the captain wanted to use every minute. After two practices, the coach asked players to rate each drill. The first drill received strong scores, but mistakes increased later. Several players said they needed a moment to drink water and check the next goal. The team tested a five-minute break after forty minutes. It kept the total practice time the same by shortening repeated instructions. In the next two practices, later drills had fewer simple mistakes. The captain learned that using every minute for movement did not always mean using the whole practice well for everyone.

MODAL_COULD.text: For the autumn school event, the environment club wanted to reduce disposable cups. One idea was to use only refill cups that visitors returned after drinking. Before changing the whole system, the club tested two drink stations for one afternoon. Station A used disposable cups. Station B gave visitors a strong cup with a return token. The students counted cups, return rates, waiting time, and the minutes needed for washing. Most refill cups came back, but the washing table became crowded just before the final performance. Disposable cups were faster but created much more trash. The club chose a mixed plan for the real event. Refill cups were used during normal hours, while one small supply of disposable cups was kept for the busiest twenty minutes and for visitors who needed them. The experiment helped the club reduce waste without creating a new service problem. After the event, the club compared its records with the previous year. Trash from drink cups had fallen, and the waiting time stayed within the limit the organizers had set. The members wrote both benefits and problems in their report so the next team could improve the plan again.

SUPERLATIVE.text: For the autumn school event, the environment club wanted to reduce disposable cups. One idea was to use only refill cups that visitors returned after drinking. Before changing the whole system, the club tested two drink stations for one afternoon. Station A used disposable cups. Station B gave visitors a strong cup with a return token. The students counted cups, return rates, waiting time, and the minutes needed for washing. Most refill cups came back, but the washing table became crowded just before the final performance. Disposable cups were faster but created much more trash. The club chose a mixed plan for the real event. Refill cups were used during normal hours, while one small supply of disposable cups was kept for the busiest twenty minutes and for visitors who needed them. The experiment helped the club reduce waste without creating a new service problem. After the event, the club compared its records with the previous year. Trash from drink cups had fallen, and the waiting time stayed within the limit the organizers had set. The members wrote both benefits and problems in their report so the next team could improve the plan again.

MODAL_COULD.text: Teachers received reports that some students could not hear the afternoon announcement. It sounded clear in the office, so the cause was not obvious. A student team tested the message in the library, at the east stairs, and in the old music hall. They wrote down which words they missed. The first two places were fine. In the music hall, the message became very quiet whenever the fire door in the connecting hallway was closed. The speaker was on the other side. The school did not leave the fire door open. It added a speaker inside the hall and repeated the test with the door closed. All three listeners then heard the complete message. The solution kept the safety rule and fixed the problem.

SUPERLATIVE.text: The student council made a survey about the school festival. Its first question asked students to choose among five detailed plans for next year. When six first-year students tested the form, three stopped at that question. They said they did not know enough about the plans. The survey team discussed the result and kept the useful question but moved it later. The new first question was simple: ‘Which part of this year's festival did you use or visit?' Later questions gave short information before asking about future choices. In a second test, all six students reached the end. Changing the order did not remove important thinking. It gave students information and confidence before the hardest question.
